set1.q: A 34-year-old woman has visible, dilated, tortuous veins of the thigh and calf that are tender to palpation, with aching heaviness after prolonged standing. Which is the most common predisposing factor for her condition?
opts: Recent pregnancy
Women are at higher risk after pregnancy, so a recent pregnancy is a recognized contributor. The question asks for the most common predisposing factor, and that is family history, not pregnancy.
Regular heavy lifting

Heavy lifting causes periods of high venous pressure and is a real risk factor for varicose veins, but it is not the most common one. Family history is named the most common predisposing factor, so it outranks lifting even in a patient who lifts.
Family history of varicose veins

Correct. Her dilated, tortuous, tender thigh and calf veins with aching heaviness after standing describe varicose veins. Among the risk factors, family history is named the most common predisposing factor for unwanted leg veins, ahead of prolonged standing, heavy lifting and pregnancy.
Prolonged standing at work

Prolonged standing produces periods of high venous pressure and also brings on her aching, but it is a contributing risk factor rather than the most common one. Family history is named the most common predisposing factor for unwanted leg veins.

set1.q: A 38-year-old woman has long-standing swelling of both legs just above the ankles that is symmetric, with normal skin color and no ulcers or varicose veins. Cardiac, kidney and liver evaluations are normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Lymphedema

Lymphedema typically causes unilateral swelling with absent varicosities and pitting edema, and brawny discoloration is rare. Her swelling is bilateral and symmetric and sits just above the ankles, the distinguishing pattern of lipedema.
Heart failure edema

Heart failure, chronic kidney disease and decompensated liver disease do cause bilateral leg edema, but her cardiac, kidney and liver evaluations are normal. With those causes excluded, symmetric swelling just above the ankles in a woman points to lipedema.
Lipedema

Correct. Bilateral, symmetric swelling just above the ankles in a woman is how lipedema is described. Her normal cardiac, kidney and liver evaluations exclude the systemic causes of bilateral edema, and the absence of varicose veins, ulcers or skin color change argues against venous disease.
Chronic venous insufficiency

Chronic venous insufficiency is the usual source of the skin changes and leg ulcers that history and examination pick up, and it is confirmed with venous duplex ultrasound. She has normal skin color, no ulcers and no varicose veins, so symmetric swelling just above the ankles fits lipedema instead.

set1.q: A 47-year-old woman has a tender, red, firm segment along a forearm vein after a peripheral intravenous catheter was removed. Venous duplex ultrasound shows a superficial vein with a thickened wall. Which additional finding would establish thrombophlebitis rather than phlebitis alone?
opts: Clot within the vein lumen

Correct. The ultrasound already shows wall thickening, which by itself means phlebitis, inflammation of the vein wall without thrombus. Clot within the vein together with that thickening establishes thrombophlebitis; duplex ultrasound, the gold standard, shows it as a noncompressible superficial vein with clot.
Thickening of the vein wall
Wall thickening is already present and is the finding both conditions share; on its own it defines phlebitis. Only the addition of clot within the vein converts the diagnosis to thrombophlebitis.
Reflux through incompetent valves

Reflux through incompetent valves is not part of how phlebitis and thrombophlebitis are told apart. Duplex ultrasound makes that call on two findings: wall thickening alone is phlebitis, and wall thickening with clot in the vein is thrombophlebitis.
Fluid collection around the vein

A fluid collection around the vein is not the criterion that separates the two conditions. Infection within the vein is suggested by high fever, fluctuance or purulent drainage, while thrombophlebitis is defined by clot inside a thickened vein.
